candidates.title: A Prospective Randomized Trial to Assess Early versus Delayed Weight Bearing Following Operatively Treated Ankle Fractures in the United States.
candidates.authors_short: Obremskey WT, Archer KR, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the safety of early versus delayed weight bearing and effectiveness for improving return-to-work following ankle fracture repair. METHODS: Design: Prospective randomized study. SETTING: 19 United States Trauma Centers. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adult patients (≥18 years) with ankle fracture (OTA/AO 44 A, B or C) undergoing surgical fixation were included. Open Gustilo-Anderson (G-A) Type IIIB, IIIC, syndesmotic injuries with fixation, and injuries with arterial impaction that surgeons felt unsafe to weight were excluded. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The co-primary outcomes were (1) non-inferiority of early versus delayed weight bearing for reoperation for complications of hardware failure, non-union, loss of reduction, infection, or fusion; and (2) gated superiority of early versus delayed weight bearing for time to return-to-work, both within 365 days of randomization. Reoperation and time to return-to-work was compared between patients assigned to early (2 weeks post-operatively) versus delayed (6 weeks post-operatively) weight bearing. RESULTS: The modified intent to treat sample included 418 patients enrolled between January 2020 through October 2023; 214 early (mean age: 47; SD (15) range (18-84); 35% male); 204 delayed (mean age: 43; SD (15); 36% male). Reoperation for complication occurred in 5 early (2.3%, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.3%, 4.4%), and 7 delayed patients (3.4%, 95% CI: 0.9%, 5.9%). Median time to return-to-work (95% CI) was 54 (42, 77) days and 69 (47, 89) days for the early and delayed groups, respectively. Early weight bearing was non-inferior to delayed weight bearing for reoperation (difference in complication free survival (early - delayed): 1.5 percentage points; 90% two sided CI: -1.7%, 4.8% which excluded the non-inferiority tolerance of -5.0%) and not superior for return-to-work (Hazard Ratio 1.1, 95% CI: 0.8, 1.6, p=0.475). CONCLUSIONS: Trial findings add to the growing evidence demonstrating the safety of early weight bearing after fixation of bimalleolar and trimalleolar ankle fracture without syndesmotic disruption, a key concern for both clinicians and patients. However, no statistically significant benefit of earlier return-to-work was found. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: I.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-impact RCT in JBJS on early vs delayed weight bearing after ankle fracture fixation across 19 US trauma centers with 418 patients, directly relevant to daily trauma practice with clear safety and return-to-work outcomes.
bullets: Early weight bearing at 2 weeks after surgical ankle fracture fixation carries the same reoperation risk as waiting until 6 weeks, with complication rates under 4% in both groups.
These findings apply to adults with operatively fixed bimalleolar and trimalleolar fractures without syndesmotic injury or open grade IIIB/IIIC wounds.
Surgeons can safely allow early weight bearing after ankle fixation, though patients should not expect a meaningful faster return to work compared to delayed protocols.

candidates.title: Comparison of Shoulder Field Anesthesia (SFA) with Interscalene Block (ISB) for Analgesia After Arthroscopic Shoulder Surgery: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Qawasmi F, Gazit T, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: An interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB) is commonly used for analgesia after shoulder surgery but is associated with neurologic and respiratory complications, including hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia (SFA) is a landmark-guided, phrenic nerve-sparing technique that may provide effective analgesia with fewer complications. The purpose of this study was to compare SFA with ISB for pain control after arthroscopic shoulder surgery. We investigated whether SFA would provide noninferior analgesia as measured by cumulative 48-hour postoperative pain scores. METHODS: In this randomized trial, patients undergoing arthroscopic shoulder surgery were assigned to SFA or ISB. Postoperative pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) at 2, 4, 8, 24, and 48 hours. Patient satisfaction was assessed at 48 hours. Other secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, hospital stay, and block-related complications. RESULTS: Eighty patients (mean age, 47.7 ± 15.7 years; 53 men) completed the study. All patients were classified as White; 80% were of Middle Eastern ethnicity. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the SFA and ISB groups. The primary outcome analysis demonstrated a mean difference in the cumulative 48-hour NRS pain score of -0.824 (ISB - SFA), with a 95% confidence interval of -1.853 to 0.206. The upper limit of the confidence interval remained below the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.5 NRS points, demonstrating noninferiority of SFA. ISB provided lower pain scores during the early postoperative period (4 to 8 hours), and pain scores converged thereafter. Hospital stay was shorter in the SFA group. Opioid consumption, patient satisfaction, and oxygen desaturation rates were similar between groups. Two cases of Horner syndrome and 1 respiratory event requiring intensive care occurred in the ISB group; none occurred in the SFA group. CONCLUSIONS: SFA was noninferior to ISB for the prespecified cumulative 48-hour pain end point. ISB provided superior pain relief during the first 4 to 8 hours, but SFA offered a lung-sparing alternative with similar cumulative opioid requirements and patient satisfaction, fewer clinically apparent block-related complications, and a shorter hospital stay. These findings support a risk-benefit framework to guide individualized analgesic selection. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level I. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review on biological age markers in adult spinal deformity surgery offers immediately actionable frailty, sarcopenia, and bone quality risk-stratification tools for preoperative planning with strong practical applicability.
bullets: Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia matched interscalene block for total pain control over 48 hours after arthroscopic shoulder surgery, though interscalene block gave better relief in the first 4 to 8 hours.
Interscalene block caused two cases of Horner syndrome and one respiratory event requiring ICU care, while shoulder field anesthesia caused none and led to a shorter hospital stay.

For patients where phrenic nerve palsy is a concern, such as those with reduced lung reserve, shoulder field anesthesia is a viable lung-sparing alternative with similar opioid use and patient satisfaction.

candidates.title: Preoperative Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor Use is Associated With Increased Complication Risk After Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Dose-Response Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Alfonsi SP, Zickler CL, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Preoperative selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) use has been associated with adverse outcomes following primary total hip arthroplasty (THA). This study examined whether complication rates vary based on SSRI daily dosage. METHODS: A claims database (2010 to 2023) identified 77,958 primary THA patients who did not have osteoporosis and who filled an SSRI prescription 60 days preoperatively. Patients were matched 1:3 to SSRI-naive individuals by age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and history of cognitive disorders, depression, anxiety, and substance use. Overall, 77,958 SSRI users were matched to 233,277 controls (mean age 65 years). After matching, baseline demographics and rates of anxiety and depression (all P > 0.13) were similar between cohorts. The SSRI doses were standardized using quantity, duration, and strength, then stratified as low (0 to 30 mg), medium (30 to 100 mg), or high (greater than 100 mg). Multivariate regression and Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed surgical complications and revision-free survival at 2-year follow-up. RESULTS: Preoperative SSRI use was associated with greater 2-year complications (5.2 versus 3.2%, P < 0.001). In adjusted multivariate analysis, SSRI use was associated with increased odds of component loosening (OR [odds ratio] 1.5), periprosthetic fracture (OR 1.8), periprosthetic joint infection (OR 1.7), dislocation (OR 2.0), and revision surgery (OR 1.7) (all P < 0.001). There was no dose-dependent relationship observed. Component loosening approached statistical significance at high SSRI doses (OR 3.7, P = 0.07). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated reduced revision-free survival among SSRI users (P < 0.001) at 2-year follow-up. CONCLUSION: Preoperative SSRI use, regardless of dose, was associated with higher 2-year rates of periprosthetic joint infection, dislocation, fracture, loosening, and revision. However, the absence of a dose-response relationship suggests that SSRIs are unlikely to be directly responsible for these complications.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large NSQIP-based study in JSES with nearly 30,000 patients developing and validating a preoperative bedside score (SHORD) for non-home discharge after TSA, directly useful for surgical planning and patient counseling.
bullets: THA patients on SSRIs preoperatively had double the dislocation risk and nearly double the infection, fracture, and revision risk compared to SSRI-naive patients at 2 years.
The elevated complication risk was consistent across low, medium, and high SSRI doses, suggesting SSRIs are likely a marker of underlying patient vulnerability rather than a direct cause.
Orthopaedic surgeons should treat preoperative SSRI use as a red flag for risk stratification in THA candidates, prompting closer perioperative monitoring regardless of the prescribed dose.

candidates.title: Defining Long-Term Success After Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty: Survivorship and Clinically Important Outcomes.
candidates.authors_short: Kucharik MP, Hung V, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term success after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA) is frequently defined by implant survivorship, but revision-free survival may not reflect durable clinical benefit. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 791 consecutive aTSAs performed between 2003 and 2015 was conducted. Implant survivorship was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Clinical outcomes were evaluated at a 10-year landmark, and clinically important thresholds for the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score were derived using patient satisfaction as the anchor. Multivariable regression identified predictors of revision and substantial clinical benefit (SCB). RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier survivorship was 96.1% at 10 years and 93.7% at 15 years. Walch B glenoid morphology and younger age were independently associated with revision. Clinical outcomes remained improved at long-term follow-up despite gradual attenuation over time. At 10 years, the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) threshold for the ASES score was 68.1, and 69.5% of shoulders achieved it. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and SCB thresholds for the change in ASES score were 14.0 and 39.2, achieved by 79.9% and 55.8% of shoulders, respectively. Younger age, primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and lower preoperative ASES score were independently associated with achievement of SCB. CONCLUSIONS: aTSA demonstrated excellent long-term implant survivorship and modest patient-reported outcomes, although shoulder function gradually attenuated over extended follow-up. Despite the gradual functional decline, most patients maintained clinically meaningful benefit at 10 years. Younger age and Walch B morphology increased revision risk. Long-term clinically important thresholds provide patient-centered benchmarks for defining durable success. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS study of 86 hips challenges the established 8-mm anterior overhang threshold for iliopsoas impingement management after THA, with direct implications for operative decision-making between tenotomy and acetabular revision.
bullets: Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty showed 96% implant survival at 10 years and 94% at 15 years, but only 56% of shoulders achieved substantial clinical benefit at the 10-year mark.

Younger patients and those with Walch B glenoid morphology face higher revision risk, while younger age, primary osteoarthritis, and lower preoperative function predict better long-term clinical outcomes.
Surgeons should counsel patients that shoulder function gradually declines over time after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty, even when the implant remains in place.

candidates.title: Mechanical Failure and Revision Risk Following Transition from PFNA to TFNA: A Single-Center Cohort Study of 1,970 Patients.
candidates.authors_short: Ben Zoor I, Fogel I, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, and time to failure between two cephalomedullary nail designs following an institutional transition. METHODS: Design: Retrospective consecutive cohort study. SETTING: Single Level I trauma center, Israel. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged >65 years with acute OTA/AO 31A fractures (subtypes 31A1-31A3) treated with a short cephalomedullary nail with helical blade fixation, either the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) or the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA), between January 2018 and May 2025 were included. Implant type was determined solely by an institutional transition from PFNA to TFNA in March 2023 for logistical reasons rather than surgeon preference. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, time to failure, body mass index (BMI), and Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) were compared between groups. Mortality within the early revision-risk window was compared between groups to exclude survival bias. RESULTS: The PFNA cohort comprised 1,388 patients (mean age 83.1 years, range 65-102; 986 females [71.0%]) and the TFNA cohort 582 patients (mean age 82.9 years, range 65-107; 407 females [69.9%]); baseline demographics were comparable (age, p=0.691; sex, p=0.626). Orthopedic follow-up was 63.9% for the TFNA cohort versus 61.0% for the PFNA cohort (p=0.24), with a shorter maximum observation period for TFNA (TFNA 26 vs. PFNA 88 months).TFNA was associated with a five-fold increase in implant mechanical failure relative to PFNA (TFNA 1.6% vs. PFNA 0.3%; RR=5.36, 95% CI 1.66-17.3; p=0.005), primarily driven by a four-fold increase in cut-outs (1.2% vs. 0.3%; RR=4.18, 95% CI 1.23-14.2; p=0.027). Failures occurred earlier with TFNA (median 80.0 vs. 244.0 days; p=0.027). Among cut-outs, OTA/AO subtype distribution did not differ (31A1: TFNA 57.1% vs. PFNA 50.0%; no 31A3 in either group; p=1.00); TFNA patients had a higher BMI (median 23.9 vs. 20.1 kg/m 2 ; p=0.024), but mean TAD did not differ (TFNA 24.6 vs. PFNA 21.1 mm; p=0.37). Mortality within the revision-risk window did not differ (TFNA 7.2% vs. PFNA 8.8%; p=0.24). CONCLUSIONS: The transition to the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA) was associated with five-fold higher mechanical failure and four-fold higher cut-out rates than the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) with earlier failures suggesting reduced mechanical stability of the TFNA during early fracture healing. Heightened vigilance is warranted when using TFNA, particularly in patients with higher body mass index early postoperatively. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review on endoscopic spine surgery evidence maturity and US adoption pathways provides a timely synthesis of comparative evidence and practical barriers highly relevant to spine surgeons considering technique adoption.
bullets: In 1,970 patients over 65 with hip fractures, switching from PFNA to TFNA was associated with a fivefold higher mechanical failure rate and a fourfold higher cut-out rate.
Failures in the TFNA group occurred much earlier after surgery (median 80 days versus 244 days), suggesting the implant is less stable during the critical early healing period.
Surgeons using TFNA, especially in heavier patients, should increase postoperative surveillance frequency in the first three months to catch failures before they become catastrophic.

candidates.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty Is Associated With Lower 90-Day Inpatient Readmission Than Hemiarthroplasty for Femoral Neck Fracture in Patients Aged 65-75 Years: A Propensity Score-Matched Nationwide Readmissions Database Study.
candidates.authors_short: Maman D, Steinfeld Y, Berkovich Y
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comparative early hospital-based outcomes of hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty (THA) for femoral neck fracture remain uncertain in patients aged 65-75 years. METHODS: Using the 2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database, we identified patients aged 65-75 years admitted with an acute femoral neck fracture who underwent hemiarthroplasty or THA. Patients were matched 1:1 using exact matching on age, Hospital Frailty Risk Score category, and mental-disorder status, plus propensity-score matching with a 0.20-standard-deviation caliper. The primary outcome was all-cause inpatient readmission within 90 days. RESULTS: Among 8,012 eligible admissions, 5,108 patients underwent hemiarthroplasty and 2,904 underwent THA. Matching yielded 2,702 patients per group, with all postmatch absolute standardized mean differences <0.10. THA was associated with a lower observed 90-day inpatient readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty (10.1% vs 15.7%; odds ratio, 0.60; 95% confidence interval, 0.51-0.71; P < .001). Death during the first readmission was also less frequent after THA (0.1% vs 0.7%; P = .002). A narrowly defined inpatient principal-diagnosis dislocation indicator did not differ significantly between groups and should not be interpreted as overall dislocation incidence. Index and total 90-day hospital charges were higher with THA. CONCLUSIONS: In this observational claims-based study, THA was associated with a lower observed 90-day inpatient readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty. Residual selection bias may partly explain this association, and these findings do not establish a causal benefit of THA. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large claims-database propensity-matched study (n=77,958) in JBJS demonstrating dose-independent SSRI-associated increases in PJI, dislocation, and revision after THA provides important preoperative medication counseling data.
bullets: In patients aged 65 to 75 with femoral neck fracture, THA was associated with a 90-day readmission rate of 10.1% compared to 15.7% for hemiarthroplasty.
Death at first readmission was also lower after THA than hemiarthroplasty (0.1% vs 0.7%), though THA carried higher index and total 90-day hospital costs.
For otherwise healthy patients aged 65 to 75 with femoral neck fracture, this data supports reconsidering hemiarthroplasty as the default implant choice, pending prospective confirmation.

candidates.title: Myocardial Infarction Within 6 Months before Total Shoulder Arthroplasty is Strongly Associated with Postoperative Complications.
candidates.authors_short: Parmar RP, Sahni VS, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: As total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) is increasing in volume, limited data exist regarding how recent myocardial infarction (MI) influences postoperative outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of MI timing, type, treatment, and anatomical location on rates of postoperative cardiac, medical, and surgical complications following TSA. METHODS: A national insurance database, PearlDiver, was queried to identify patients with a history of MI within two years prior to TSA. These patients were propensity-matched 1:4 to controls without prior MI based on demographics and comorbidities. The MI cohort was stratified by timing (0-6 months, 6-12 months, 12-18 months, 18-24 months), and subgroup analyses were performed by MI type (Type 1 vs. Type 2), ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) vs Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) classification, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), and infarct location. RESULTS: A history of MI within 2 years preceding TSA had a strong association with higher odds of postoperative MI (OR 5.67; 95% CI, 3.86-8.32). The strongest association was observed when MI occurred within 6 months of TSA (OR 9.95; 95% CI, 6.50-15.24). Type 1 MI was strongly associated with postoperative MI, particularly within 6 months (OR 10.86; 95% CI, 6.96-16.95). Type 2 MI within 6 months was strongly associated with postoperative MI (OR 10.69; 95% CI, 2.50-45.63), DVT (OR 9.81; 95% CI, 2.30-41.79), and PJI (OR 5.24; 95% CI, 1.60-17.18). Both STEMI (OR = 6.17) and NSTEMI (OR = 5.77) were strongly associated with postoperative MI. Anterior MI was strongly associated with postoperative MI (OR 7.22; 95% CI, 3.36-15.49), whereas inferior MI was strongly associated with 90-day mortality (OR 6.46; 95% CI, 1.85-22.60). CONCLUSION: MI within 2 years and specifically 6 months of TSA was associated with higher odds of postoperative complications. MI timing, subtype, treatment, and location should be carefully weighed when considering TSA in this high-risk population.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS study of 791 consecutive aTSAs defining long-term survivorship, PASS, MCID, and SCB thresholds at 10-15 years fills a critical evidence gap for counseling patients on expected outcomes after anatomic shoulder arthroplasty.
bullets: Patients who had a heart attack within 6 months before total shoulder arthroplasty were nearly 10 times more likely to suffer a postoperative heart attack than matched controls.
The elevated risk applies regardless of heart attack type, with anterior infarcts linked to postoperative cardiac events and inferior infarcts linked to 90-day mortality.
Surgeons should carefully weigh the timing and location of a prior heart attack before proceeding with elective total shoulder arthroplasty, particularly within the 6-month window.

candidates.title: Lateral Opening-Wedge Versus Medial Closing-Wedge Distal Femoral Osteotomy for Adolescent Idiopathic Genu Valgum: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Khatri JP, Ghosh AK, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Distal femoral osteotomy is used to correct symptomatic genu valgum after distal femoral physeal closure, but comparative evidence between lateral opening-wedge osteotomy (LOW) and medial closing-wedge osteotomy (MCW) in adolescents is limited. We compared radiographic correction, recovery, and complications between the techniques. METHODS: In this prospective randomised trial, 65 adolescents aged 12 to 18 years with idiopathic genu valgum and radiographic closure of the distal femoral physis were allocated 1:1 to LOW or MCW. Three participants were lost to follow-up, leaving 62 participants for the available-case analysis (LOW, n=32; MCW, n=30). In bilateral cases, only the first operated limb was analyzed. The primary outcome was signed mechanical axis deviation (MAD) at radiographic union; unadjusted comparisons were the primary focus, and covariate-adjusted analyses were supportive. RESULTS: MAD at union was 6.8±6.2 mm after LOW and 2.4±5.3 mm after MCW (LOW minus MCW, 4.4 mm; 95% CI: 1.5-7.3; P=0.003). The supportive adjusted difference was 3.0 mm (95% CI: -0.4 to 6.5; P=0.08). Absolute deviation from neutral was 6.8±6.2 versus 4.0±4.1 mm (difference, 2.8 mm; 95% CI: 0.2-5.5; P=0.04). At union, mLDFA did not differ significantly; aLDFA favored MCW in the unadjusted analysis, but neither adjusted angular difference was significant. One-year Pedi-IKDC scores, pain, satisfaction, union time, hospital stay, and return to activity did not differ between groups. Unique symptomatic lateral plate/iliotibial-band irritation occurred in 4 of 32 LOW participants (13%) and 3 of 30 MCW participants (10%; P=1.00). CONCLUSIONS: MAD at radiographic union favored MCW, but the trial did not establish clinically meaningful superiority. The adjusted estimate was smaller and nonsignificant, and no sustained functional advantage was detected. Both techniques produced substantial correction with favorable short- to mid-term outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I-therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective multicenter cohort (91 patients, PLUTO Study Group) in AJSM demonstrating minimal clinically significant alignment change after transphyseal ACLR near skeletal maturity provides important safety evidence for a common surgical dilemma.
bullets: In adolescents with idiopathic genu valgum, medial closing-wedge distal femoral osteotomy achieved slightly better mechanical axis alignment at union than lateral opening-wedge, but the difference was small and lost significance after adjustment.
Functional outcomes, pain, satisfaction, union time, and return to activity were equivalent between the two techniques at one year.
Either technique is a reasonable choice for adolescents with physeal-closed symptomatic genu valgum, as both produce reliable correction without a clear clinical winner.

candidates.title: Effects of Early Rehabilitation on Shoulder Joint Stiffness and Functional Recovery Following Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair.
candidates.authors_short: Shou S, He L, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association between rehabilitation initiation timing and shoulder stiffness and functional recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR). METHODS: Patients who underwent ARCR between January 2019 and January 2023 were retrospectively identified. Based on documented rehabilitation initiation time, patients were classified post hoc into early (n = 64) or delayed rehabilitation groups (n = 71). The primary outcome was shoulder stiffness at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included Constant and American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) scores, visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, and passive forward flexion. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used for sensitivity analysis. Subgroup analyses assessed whether the observed association varied by patient characteristics. RESULTS: Among 135 patients, early rehabilitation was associated with less shoulder stiffness at 3 months and more favorable outcomes during follow-up, including higher Constant and ASES scores, lower VAS pain scores, and greater passive forward flexion. Linear mixed-effects models demonstrated significant improvements over time in all outcomes, although the overall group-by-time interactions were not statistically significant. The estimated between-group difference in passive forward flexion was greatest at 3 months. IPTW analysis generally supported the primary findings. CONCLUSION: Early rehabilitation was associated with less shoulder stiffness and earlier recovery of shoulder function and passive forward flexion after ARCR. These observational findings do not establish causality. Randomized trials with systematic monitoring of repair integrity and adverse events are needed to determine the effectiveness and safety of early rehabilitation.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review on cervical sagittal alignment principles directly applicable to surgical planning with clear evidence-based alignment parameters linked to patient-reported outcomes and adjacent-segment disease risk.
bullets: Patients who started rehabilitation early after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair had less shoulder stiffness at 3 months and better pain and functional scores throughout follow-up.
The benefit was most apparent in passive forward flexion at 3 months, and results held after statistical adjustment for baseline differences between groups.
For surgeons repairing rotator cuffs, earlier rehab initiation appears favorable, but this is observational data and randomized trials are still needed before changing protocol.

candidates.title: Bleeding and Hemostasis Optimization in Primary and Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Structured Expert-Opinion Survey.
candidates.authors_short: Chen AF, Mont MA, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Disruptive bleeding following total knee arthroplasty (TKA) continues to affect postoperative recovery despite advances in perioperative blood management, with wound drainage and dressing-related findings common clinical concerns. Conventional definitions based on estimated blood loss or hemoglobin decline may not capture bleeding events that alter clinical management. This study sought to establish agreement on disruptive bleeding in TKA and identify clinically relevant factors guiding monitoring, escalation, and hemostatic decision-making. METHODS: A survey-based study was conducted among 14 fellowship-trained arthroplasty surgeons who had experience in primary and revision TKA. Domains included risk factors, definitions of disruptive bleeding, intraoperative bleeding patterns, postoperative drainage assessment, escalation criteria, and the use of topical hemostatic agents. Responses included Likert-scale ratings, categorical selections, and free-text data. High agreement for items was defined a priori as ≥ 70% agreement. RESULTS: Respondents supported defining disruptive bleeding as a composite of clinically meaningful outcomes rather than isolated quantitative measures. There was unanimous agreement to include operational indicators (symptomatic hemoglobin decline greater than three g/dL and persistent wound drainage) and downstream events (transfusion, reoperation, embolization, and readmission). Thrombocytopenia and anticoagulant use were important risk factors (n = 14 of 14), followed by coagulopathy and liver disease (n = 12 of 14). Escalation triggers included suspected arterial bleeding (n = 14 of 14), expanding hematoma (n = 13 of 14), hemodynamic instability (n = 13 of 14), neurovascular compromise (n = 13 of 14), and drainage beyond postoperative day five (n = 12 of 14). Routine prophylactic use of topical hemostatic agents was not supported in primary TKA (n = 2 of 14), but was selectively favored in revision cases (n = 7 of 14). Variability remained regarding drainage thresholds and timing of intervention. CONCLUSIONS: Disruptive bleeding in TKA was viewed as a composite construct defined by events that alter care rather than isolated numeric blood-loss measures. These findings represent an exploratory, hypothesis-generating framework requiring multidisciplinary and data-driven validation.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review on osteochondral lesions of the talus provides a contemporary, evidence-based treatment algorithm with clear stratification by lesion characteristics, directly guiding surgical decision-making for a common and challenging condition.
bullets: Expert consensus defines disruptive bleeding after TKA by clinical events that change management, including hemoglobin drop over 3 g/dL, persistent wound drainage, transfusion, reoperation, or readmission, not by blood loss numbers alone.
In patients with thrombocytopenia, anticoagulant use, coagulopathy, or liver disease, surgeons should have a lower threshold for monitoring and escalation after primary or revision TKA.

Routine topical haemostatic agents are not supported in primary TKA but may be appropriate selectively in revision cases, and arterial bleeding, expanding haematoma, haemodynamic instability, or drainage past day five should prompt escalation.
